title: Power Electronics
tagline: Power semiconductors, rectifiers, DC–DC converters, inverters and converter control
summary: Power electronics processes electrical energy efficiently with switches. This course covers power semiconductor devices, rectifiers, non-isolated and isolated DC–DC converters, inverters and pulse-width modulation, the dynamics and control of converters, magnetic and thermal design, and applications from phone chargers to motor drives and solar inverters.
overview: Power electronics is the technology of converting electrical energy from one form to another — AC to DC, DC to DC at a different voltage, DC to AC at a controlled frequency — using semiconductor switches rather than resistors or linear transistors. A switch that is either fully on (small voltage across it) or fully off (no current through it) dissipates almost nothing, so a converter built from switches, inductors and capacitors can approach $100\,\%$ efficiency. That single idea powers phone chargers and laptop adapters, the voltage regulators beside every processor, variable-speed motor drives, solar and wind inverters, electric-vehicle traction and charging, and high-voltage DC links between grids.

The course begins with the switches themselves — diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs, thyristors and the newer silicon-carbide and gallium-nitride devices — and with what it costs to turn them on and off. It then builds the main converter families: line-frequency rectifiers and their harmonics, the buck, boost and buck–boost DC–DC converters, isolated converters with high-frequency transformers, and voltage-source inverters with pulse-width modulation. The second half treats converters as systems: averaged and small-signal models, feedback control with voltage-mode and current-mode loops, the design of inductors, transformers and heat sinks, and finally complete applications in drives, renewable energy, vehicles and the grid.

The analysis rests on a few principles used again and again: in periodic steady state an inductor's average voltage and a capacitor's average current are zero (volt-second and charge balance); small ripple can be neglected to first order; and a switching circuit can be replaced by its average over a switching period. What makes the subject demanding is that a real converter is never only a circuit problem — losses, parasitic inductance, magnetic saturation, temperature and electromagnetic interference decide whether a design on paper works on the bench. Work every waveform by hand, check each result against the energy balance, and keep asking where the losses go.
outcomes: Compare power diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs, thyristors and wide-bandgap devices and select a switch for a given voltage, current and frequency.
Estimate conduction and switching losses of a hard-switched power stage and design a basic gate drive.
Analyse single- and three-phase diode and thyristor rectifiers, including output voltage, harmonics, commutation overlap and power factor.
Derive the conversion ratios and ripples of buck, boost and buck–boost converters in continuous and discontinuous conduction using volt-second and charge balance.
Design isolated flyback, forward and bridge converters, including the transformer turns ratio and core reset.
Explain single- and three-phase voltage-source inverters and compare sinusoidal, third-harmonic and space-vector PWM.
Derive averaged and small-signal models of DC–DC converters and design voltage-mode and current-mode feedback compensators.
Design an inductor and a transformer for a converter, and size a heat sink from a thermal-resistance model.
Describe the power-electronic architecture of motor drives, photovoltaic and wind converters, battery chargers, electric vehicles and grid-connected systems.

history.title: Mercury-arc rectifier
history.detail: Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury-arc rectifier, which for half a century supplied DC for electric railways, electrochemistry and, later, the first HVDC links.

history.title: The p-n-p-n transistor switch
history.detail: John Moll, Morris Tanenbaum, James Goldey and Nick Holonyak at Bell Labs described the silicon p-n-p-n switch, the basis of the thyristor.

history.title: Commercial silicon-controlled rectifier
history.detail: General Electric introduced the silicon-controlled rectifier (SCR), which began the replacement of mercury-arc valves and motor–generator sets by solid-state converters.

history.title: PWM inverter drive
history.detail: Arnold Schönung and Herbert Stemmler of Brown Boveri published the sine–triangle (subharmonic) pulse-width modulation of a variable-frequency inverter for AC motor drives.

history.title: Field-oriented control
history.detail: Felix Blaschke of Siemens published the principle of field orientation, which lets an inverter control an induction motor's torque as quickly as that of a DC machine.

history.title: Power electronics named as a discipline
history.detail: William E. Newell's keynote at the Power Electronics Specialists Conference described power electronics as the field at the intersection of power, electronics and control.

history.title: State-space averaging
history.detail: R. D. Middlebrook and Slobodan Ćuk presented state-space averaging, the standard method for modelling the dynamics of switching converters.

history.title: Insulated-gate bipolar transistor
history.detail: B. Jayant Baliga and colleagues at General Electric reported the insulated-gate transistor, which combines a MOS gate with bipolar conduction and became the workhorse switch of drives and inverters.

history.title: Space-vector modulation
history.detail: Heinz Willi van der Broeck, Hans-Christoph Skudelny and Georg Stanke published the analysis and realisation of space-vector PWM for three-phase inverters.

history.title: Silicon-carbide power devices
history.detail: Infineon released the first commercial silicon-carbide Schottky diodes; SiC MOSFETs followed from Cree in 2011, and GaN transistors entered the market around 2010, opening the wide-bandgap era.

references.title: Fundamentals of Power Electronics
references.authors: Robert W. Erickson and Dragan Maksimović
references.note: Third edition. The standard text for DC–DC converters, averaged modelling, control and magnetics design; the notation of this course follows it.

references.title: Power Electronics: Converters, Applications, and Design
references.authors: Ned Mohan, Tore M. Undeland and William P. Robbins
references.note: Third edition. Broad coverage of rectifiers, inverters, drives and devices, with practical design detail.

references.title: Principles of Power Electronics
references.authors: John G. Kassakian, David J. Perreault, George C. Verghese and Martin F. Schlecht
references.note: Second edition. Rigorous treatment of switching circuits, dynamics and components from MIT.

references.title: Elements of Power Electronics
references.note: Second edition. Builds every converter from switching-function principles; good on rectifiers and inverters.

references.title: Fundamentals of Power Semiconductor Devices
references.note: Second edition. Device physics of power diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs, thyristors and SiC and GaN devices.

references.title: Pulse Width Modulation for Power Converters: Principles and Practice
references.authors: D. Grahame Holmes and Thomas A. Lipo
references.note: The reference on carrier-based and space-vector PWM and its harmonics.

references.title: Transformer and Inductor Design Handbook
references.note: Fourth edition. Step-by-step design of magnetic components with core and wire data.
